text: Lee is my former landlord, and we have a dispute over my $1,800 security deposit. Lee is refusing to return the money, claiming it is needed for repainting and a new living room carpet. I want the full amount back because the flat was left in good condition. I had the place professionally cleaned before moving out on 31 August and I have the receipt to prove it. Furthermore, the move-in inspection report signed by both Lee and me already describes the walls as scuffed and the carpet as stained and worn. The carpet was already eight years old when I moved in, so it was well past its prime. Lee mentions some red wine stains that appeared while I lived there, but that should not matter given the original state of the flooring. It seems unfair to charge me for replacing an old carpet and painting walls that were already scuffed when I first arrived. The evidence from the initial report shows that the property was already in this condition.

Sam is my former tenant, and we have a dispute over a $1,800 security deposit. Sam moved out on 31 August, and I am keeping the full amount to pay for repainting and a replacement carpet in the living room. Several red wine stains appeared on the living room carpet during Sam's tenancy, and Sam mounted a television on the wall without asking, which left six large anchor holes. Sam claims that the carpet was already eight years old when they moved in, but that does not really matter. Sam also mentions that the move-in inspection report, which both of us signed, describes the carpet as stained and worn and the walls as scuffed, though I am not sure that is relevant here. Sam wants the whole deposit back, but the damage to the carpet and the walls needs to be addressed.

Riley is my tenant, and we have a dispute over $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. Riley only paid $400 that month and claims this is fair compensation because the central heating failed. Riley says the house was without working heating for five weeks in January and February, but that does not seem right. Once a technician visited, the fault was diagnosed the same day. The rest of the delay was caused by a part on back order. While the repair was pending, I lent Riley two electric heaters at no charge. Riley first raised the fault in a phone call, but they and I disagree about the date of that call and about how long I took to respond. I want the $1,200 paid in full.

Morgan is my landlord, and we have a dispute over $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. The house was without working central heating for five weeks in January and February, so I only paid $400 of the rent for that month as fair compensation. My electricity bill was about $260 higher than usual because I had to use electric heaters. I first raised the fault in a phone call, but Morgan and I disagree about the date of that call and how long Morgan took to respond. Morgan claims that once a technician visited, the fault was diagnosed the same day and the rest of the delay was just because a part was on back order, but I am not sure about that. Morgan wants the $1,200 paid, but I believe the deduction is justified given the situation.

Casey is my former landlord, and we have a dispute over $4,400 for the remaining four months of a lease. I moved out after eight months to take a job in another city. Casey says the lease was for a fixed twelve months and has no early termination clause, but I am not sure that matters now. I gave Casey sixty days of written notice before leaving the flat. I also left the place clean and offered to help show it to prospective tenants to make the transition easier. A new tenant actually moved in only two weeks after I left and is paying $1,150 a month, which is more than my original rent of $1,100. Because Casey found a replacement so quickly and is making more money from the property, I do not believe I should have to pay for the months I was not living there. I have refused to pay the $4,400 because the flat was re-rented almost immediately.

Quinn is my landlord, and we have a dispute over $950 for bedbug treatment in my flat. I emailed Quinn the day I found the bedbugs and waited ten days for a response before hiring a pest control company. According to the lease, Quinn is responsible for pest control in the building. I also know that two other tenants reported bedbugs to Quinn in the two months before I did. Quinn has refused to reimburse me for the cost. Quinn claims they have a contract with a firm that would have treated the flat for $400, but I am not sure that matters. I reported the issue promptly and Quinn simply did not reply, so I had to handle the situation myself to protect my home. I am seeking the full $950 that I paid to the company.

Avery is my tenant, and we have a dispute over a $950 reimbursement request for bedbug treatment. I have refused to pay this because Avery brought a second-hand upholstered armchair into the flat a month before the bedbugs appeared. Furthermore, I have a contract with a pest control firm that would have treated the flat for $400, so the amount Avery spent is excessive. Avery claims they emailed me and waited ten days for a reply before hiring their own company, but I am not sure that is relevant. There is also some mention that two other tenants in the building reported bedbugs in the two months before Avery did, though I doubt that matters here. I believe Avery is responsible for the infestation due to the furniture they brought in, and I certainly should not be paying for an expensive private company when I already have a professional service in place for a much lower cost.

Drew is my former employer, and we have a dispute over $3,200 in unpaid overtime from my last six months as a kitchen supervisor before I resigned in June. I was rostered for 22 weekend events during that time, and two former colleagues are willing to confirm that supervisors regularly stayed late after these events to clean up. I kept a personal log of these extra hours, although I didn't show it to anyone back then. Drew claims nothing is owed, though Drew does remember saying something about making it up to the team, but it is unclear what was meant. Drew might point to my contract which describes the role as salaried with occasional weekend work included, but that doesn't seem to change the fact that I worked significant extra time. I am certain that the amount is owed despite Drew's position that nothing is due.

Jamie is my former employee, and we have a dispute regarding a claim for $3,200 in unpaid overtime from the last six months before Jamie resigned in June. I believe nothing is owed. Jamie's contract describes the role as salaried, with occasional weekend work included. While Jamie was employed, they never raised the issue of overtime pay in writing. Jamie kept a personal log of extra hours, but they never showed it to anyone at the time. I remember saying something about making it up to the team, but I cannot recall exactly what was meant. Jamie mentions that event schedules show they were rostered on 22 weekend events during those six months, but that does not seem relevant to the agreement. This situation is frustrating because the terms of the salary were clear from the start, and the sudden claim for thousands of dollars after leaving the company is unexpected.

Skyler is my former employee, and we have a dispute regarding a $6,000 signing bonus that I want Skyler to repay. The offer letter clearly states that the signing bonus is repayable in full if the employee leaves within twelve months, and Skyler resigned after only ten months. On top of that, I paid a recruiter $9,000 to fill the role. Skyler claims the bonus should not be repaid because the firm cut salaries by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away, which they argue materially changed the terms of employment. Skyler also mentions that their work changed from software development to customer support after five months. I do not believe these points are relevant or valid reasons to ignore the agreement in the offer letter. Skyler has refused to pay back the $6,000 despite the clear terms we both agreed to when they joined the firm.

Reese is my former employer, and we are in a dispute over a $6,000 signing bonus that Reese wants me to repay. I refused because the terms of my employment were materially changed. After five months, my work was changed from software development to customer support. Later, the firm cut every salary by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away. My offer letter states the bonus does not need to be repaid if the firm materially changes the terms of employment. I also worked the full notice period and trained a replacement. Reese claims that the offer letter says the signing bonus is repayable in full if the employee leaves within twelve months, but I am not sure that applies here given the circumstances. I resigned after ten months because of those changes, so I do not believe I owe the $6,000.

Kai is my former employer, and we have a dispute regarding an unpaid commission of $8,500. I sold equipment for Kai's distributor on a base salary plus commission before resigning in March. I introduced the customer to the firm and ran all the product demonstrations myself. Emails show that the customer agreed to the price with me in February. According to the commission plan, commission is earned when the customer accepts a quote, and this customer accepted my written quote by email two weeks before I resigned. A large order from this customer was then signed in April, but Kai has refused to pay me. Kai might argue that it matters that a colleague handled the final contract terms and the delivery schedule after I left, but that does not change the fact that I did the work to secure the deal. I am entitled to the commission because the quote was accepted while I was still employed.

Rowan is my former employee and we have a dispute over an $8,500 commission. Rowan resigned in March, but a large order from a customer Rowan worked with was signed in April. I have refused to pay this because a colleague handled the final contract terms and the delivery schedule after Rowan left. The firm already paid that colleague a $2,000 bonus for closing the order. Rowan claims they deserve the money because they introduced the customer and ran product demonstrations, but that is not the main issue here. Rowan also mentions that the commission plan says commission is earned when a customer accepts a quote, and they claim the customer accepted a written quote by email two weeks before Rowan resigned in March. I am not sure that is how it works or if it really matters. The fact is that the deal was finalized after Rowan was gone and someone else did the work to get it across the finish line.

Finley is my former employee, and we have a dispute over the repayment of $2,400. I paid for Finley to take a certification course and even gave Finley eight paid study days to complete it. We had a verbal agreement that Finley would stay at the clinic for at least a year after finishing, but Finley left only four months later. Now, Finley is using that certification at a rival clinic nearby. Finley claims they only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic, but I believe the agreement was clear. Finley might argue that the clinic used the certification to attract patients and that Finley treated patients under it for four months, but that is not the main point here. Regardless, I am asking for the $2,400 back since the investment was meant to benefit my business long-term, yet Finley took those skills to a competitor almost immediately. Finley has refused to pay the money back.

Emery is my former employer, and we have a dispute over $2,400. Emery wants me to repay the cost of a certification course the clinic paid for because I left four months after finishing it. I don't believe I owe this money. The clinic uses staff certifications to attract patients, and I treated patients under that qualification for four months. When I gave notice and during my exit meeting, nobody mentioned anything about repayment. Emery claims I verbally agreed to stay for at least a year, but I only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic. Emery also mentions that I was given eight paid study days, but that doesn't seem relevant to whether I have to pay the money back. I have refused to pay the $2,400 because there was no formal agreement that this was a loan or a conditional benefit.

I am having a dispute with my ex-partner, Robin, over a car we bought for $18,000 while we lived together. The car is now worth about $10,000, and since Robin has kept it, I am asking for $5,000, which is half of its current value. Robin has refused to pay anything. I paid $6,000 of the deposit from my own savings, and while we were together, the loan repayments came out of a joint account that both Robin and I paid into. Robin claims that they paid for all the insurance, servicing and repairs since we bought the car, but that does not seem relevant. Robin also mentions that the car is registered in Robin's name only and that since our separation in the spring, Robin alone paid off the remaining $7,000 of the loan, but I am doubtful about how that affects the split. I just want my fair share of the vehicle's current value.

Lee is my former landlord, and we have a dispute regarding my $1,800 security deposit. I moved out of the one-bedroom flat on 31 August, and Lee is refusing to return the money, claiming it is needed for a replacement carpet in the living room and repainting. I want the whole deposit back because the move-in inspection report, which Lee and I both signed, already describes the walls as scuffed and the carpet as stained and worn. Furthermore, the carpet was already eight years old when I moved in. I also had the flat professionally cleaned before leaving and I have the receipt to prove it. Lee mentions that the carpet needs replacing, and while they claim some red wine stains appeared during my tenancy, that does not seem like a valid reason to keep the full amount given the original condition of the property. The flat was left in a fair state, and the charges for painting and new flooring are unjustified.

Dana is my ex-partner and we have a dispute over a car we bought for $18,000 while living together. Dana is asking me for $5,000, which they say is half of the car's current $10,000 value, but I have refused to pay. The car is registered in my name only and I have paid for all the insurance, servicing, and repairs since we bought it. I also used the car every day for work while Dana rarely drove it. Since we separated in the spring, I alone have paid off the remaining $7,000 of the loan. Dana mentions that they paid $6,000 of the deposit from savings, but I am not sure that is relevant here. I believe it is unfair for Dana to ask for money now given that I have handled all the costs and the final loan payments myself.

Sage is my ex-partner and we have a dispute over a credit card balance of $7,200. I am asking Sage to pay half, which is $3,600, but Sage has refused. Much of the spending on the card was for groceries, furniture, and a holiday we took together. Since we separated, I have been paying all the interest alone. After the separation, Sage sent me a message accepting that half of the balance was Sage's responsibility and promising to pay it. Sage mentions that the card is only in my name and that Sage never had a card on the account, but I am not sure that matters since the spending benefited both of us. We were together for three years and shared a flat, and it is only fair that Sage pays their share of the joint expenses we accrued.

Jordan is my former tenant and we have a dispute over $4,400 for the remaining four months of a lease. Jordan signed a twelve-month lease at $1,100 a month but moved out after eight months for a job in another city. The lease runs for a fixed twelve months and has no early termination clause, so Jordan should pay the balance. I also paid $300 to advertise the flat again. Jordan claims that giving sixty days of written notice matters, but I am not sure it does. They also mentioned that a new tenant moved in two weeks after Jordan left and pays $1,150 a month, but that does not really change the terms of the original agreement. Jordan has refused to pay any of the money owed for the rest of the lease term.

Jules is my ex-partner and we have a dispute over $2,100. Two years ago, Jules and I adopted a dog together and both names are on the adoption papers. We separated in January and the dog lives with me, though Jules still has the dog every other weekend. In March, the dog needed emergency surgery that cost $4,200, which I paid in full. I am asking Jules for half of that cost, but Jules has refused to pay. Before we separated, we usually split vet costs, although not always evenly, but we have not discussed these expenses since January. Jules claims that it is an issue that I did not contact Jules before agreeing to the surgery, but I am not sure that really matters given the emergency. I believe it is fair for Jules to contribute since we are both owners.

Noel is my ex-partner and we have a dispute over a $2,100 bill for a dog we adopted together two years ago. We separated in January, and the dog lives with Noel. In March, the dog needed emergency surgery that cost $4,200, which Noel paid. Noel wants me to pay half, but I have refused. Noel did not contact me before agreeing to the surgery. After the separation, I offered to take the dog full-time, but Noel said no. We have not discussed vet costs since separating. Before that, we usually split them, though not always evenly. Noel mentions that both our names are on the adoption papers, but I am not sure that matters here.

Reese is my former employer, and we have a dispute regarding a $6,000 signing bonus that Reese wants me to repay. I refuse to pay it back because the firm materially changed my terms of employment. After five months, my work was changed from software development to customer support. Later, the firm cut every salary by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away, which is why I resigned. My offer letter states that the bonus does not need to be repaid if the firm materially changes the terms of employment. I also worked my full notice period and trained a replacement. Reese claims that the offer letter says the bonus is repayable in full if the employee leaves within twelve months, but I am not sure that applies here given the circumstances. I believe the changes to my role and pay make the repayment demand invalid.

Ari is my ex-fiance, and we have a dispute over a $1,800 payment. Ari wants me to pay half of a $3,600 non-refundable venue deposit that Ari paid after we broke off the engagement four months before the date. I don't think this is fair because Ari was the one who ended the engagement. Also, Ari's parents gave Ari the $3,600 specifically as a wedding gift to pay the deposit, and they have already said they do not want the money back. On top of that, I paid about $1,200 for the engagement party, and Ari did not contribute anything toward that cost. Ari mentions that we chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, but that doesn't really matter much in this situation. I do not believe I should have to pay this money given the circumstances and the fact that the deposit was a gift from Ari's parents.

Rowan is my former employee, and we have a dispute regarding an $8,500 commission on a large order. Rowan resigned in March, but the order was not signed until April. After Rowan left, a colleague handled the final contract terms and the delivery schedule, and the firm paid that colleague a $2,000 bonus for closing the order. Rowan claims they are owed the money because they introduced the customer and ran the product demonstrations, but that is not the main issue. Rowan also mentions that the commission plan says commission is earned when a customer accepts a quote, and they claim the customer accepted a written quote by email two weeks before Rowan resigned in March. I am not sure that is how it works or if it really matters here. Since the deal was finalized after Rowan was gone and another staff member did the work to close it, I have refused to pay the commission.

Emery is my former employer, and we have a dispute regarding a request for me to repay $2,400 for a certification course the clinic paid for. I refuse to pay this because the clinic used my certification to attract patients, and I treated people under that qualification for four months. When I gave notice and attended my exit meeting, nobody mentioned anything about repayment. Emery claims I verbally agreed to stay for at least a year after the course, but I only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic. Emery also mentions that I was given eight paid study days, but I am not sure that is relevant here. I do not believe I owe this money since there was no formal agreement to pay it back.

Jamie is my former employee, and we have a dispute over a claim for $3,200 in unpaid overtime from the last six months before Jamie resigned in June. Jamie says this money is owed for weekend events, but I believe nothing is owed. Jamie's contract describes the role as salaried, which includes occasional weekend work. While Jamie kept a personal log of extra hours, they never showed it to anyone at the time and never raised the issue of overtime pay in writing while employed. I remember saying something about making it up to the team, but I am not sure what was meant by that. Jamie claims the event schedules show they were rostered for 22 weekend events during that period, but that does not really matter given the terms of the employment. I am not sure why this is being raised now since there was no mention of it during the eighteen months Jamie worked as a kitchen supervisor.

Jude is my ex-partner and we have a dispute over $2,600. I paid $5,200 for our twelve-year-old child's orthodontic treatment and I am asking Jude for half of that cost, but Jude has refused to pay. The child's dentist recommended the treatment in writing, and our written separation agreement states that health and dental costs for the child are shared equally. I emailed Jude the treatment plan and price a month before it started and Jude replied saying that was fine. Jude earns somewhat more than I do. Jude has mentioned that I chose a private clinic and that a clinic covered by Jude's dental plan would have done the same treatment for about $2,000 in total, but I am not sure that matters since the agreement was already reached.

Lee is my former landlord and we have a dispute regarding my $1,800 security deposit. I moved out on 31 August and Lee told me that all of the money will be kept to pay for repainting and a replacement carpet in the living room. I want the whole deposit back because the move-in inspection report, which Lee and I both signed, already describes the walls as scuffed and the carpet as stained and worn. Additionally, the carpet was already eight years old when I moved in. I also had the flat professionally cleaned before leaving and I have the receipt to prove it. Lee mentions that some red wine stains appeared on the living room carpet during my tenancy, but that does not seem like a significant issue given the original condition of the flooring. It is unfair for Lee to keep the entire amount for wear and tear that was already documented when I first started renting the flat.

Marley is my client who owns a bakery, and we have a dispute over a final payment of $4,000 for an online ordering site I built for $10,000. Marley already paid $6,000, but they are refusing to pay the remaining balance. The site has been live and taking orders for six weeks. During the project, Marley asked for three additional features, which I built at no extra charge. Regarding the payment, the contract does not actually define what counts as finished. There is a checkout problem, but that comes from the bakery's payment provider, and nobody has even tested that. Marley mentions that the site launched five weeks later than the date in the contract, but that does not really matter now. I have invoiced the final $4,000 and believe the work is complete.

Finley is my former employee, and we have a dispute regarding the repayment of $2,400. I paid for Finley to take a certification course and even gave Finley eight paid study days to complete it. We had a verbal agreement that Finley would stay at the clinic for at least a year after finishing the course, but Finley left only four months later. Now, Finley is using that certification at a rival clinic nearby. Finley claims they only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic, but I believe the agreement was clear. Finley might argue that the clinic used the certification to attract patients and that Finley treated patients under it for four months, but that is not the main point here. Regardless, Finley has refused to pay back the $2,400 that I spent on their professional development. It feels unfair that I funded this training only for Finley to take those skills directly to a competitor so shortly after the course ended.

I hired Devon, a freelance web developer, to build an online ordering site for $10,000. I have paid $6,000, but I am refusing to pay the final $4,000 invoice because of several issues. First, the site launched five weeks later than the date in the contract. Also, some customers have complained to me that the checkout page freezes on phones. The contract does not actually define what counts as finished. Devon says the checkout problem comes from the bakery's payment provider, but nobody has tested that. Devon claims the site has been live and taking orders for six weeks, but that does not really matter given the technical flaws. I believe the work is incomplete and the delays are unacceptable. I cannot justify paying the remaining balance when the site is not functioning correctly for mobile users and the delivery was late. Devon insists the payment is due, but the quality of the final product is not where it needs to be.

I have a dispute with Blake, my ex-fiance, regarding a $1,800 refund. We booked a wedding venue together and both signed the booking form, but we broke off the engagement four months before the date. I paid the non-refundable deposit of $3,600, and I am asking Blake to pay half of that loss. Blake has refused to pay. I also lost $500 on a clothing order for the wedding, but I am not asking for any of that money back. Blake claims it does not matter because I was the one who ended the engagement, though I am not sure that is relevant here. Additionally, Blake mentioned that my parents gave me the $3,600 specifically as a wedding gift and do not want it back, but that does not seem to change the fact that we chose the venue together. I just believe it is fair that Blake covers half of the deposit we both agreed to.

I hired Lane as my wedding photographer and we are in a dispute over a $1,500 refund. I paid Lane $3,000, but I am asking for half back because I am unhappy with the result. There are no photos of the speeches or the first dance. Also, the edited photos arrived ten weeks after the wedding, even though the contract promised six. Lane says that the reception ran ninety minutes behind schedule and that the first dance and speeches happened after the contracted finish time. Lane also claims that I declined an offer to pay an overtime fee on the night, but that does not really matter. Lane mentioned that they delivered 480 edited photos instead of the 300 promised in the contract, but I am not sure that makes up for the missing moments. Lane has refused to give me any refund.

Harper is my client, and we have a dispute over a $1,500 refund they are requesting from the $3,000 fee I was paid to photograph their wedding. I have refused this request. I delivered 480 edited photos, which is well over the 300 promised in the contract. Harper actually posted many of these photos online and included a comment praising them. Regarding the event, the reception ran ninety minutes behind schedule, meaning the speeches and first dance happened after my contracted finish time. On the night, Harper declined my offer to stay longer for an overtime fee. Harper claims there are no photos of the speeches or the first dance, but that is not really the main issue here. I believe I fulfilled my obligations despite the scheduling delays caused by the client. I provided more content than required and the quality was clearly appreciated by Harper when they shared the images publicly. I do not feel a refund is justified given the circumstances and the amount of work delivered.

Shay is my client, and we have a dispute over a final payment of $5,500 for a bathroom renovation that cost $16,500 in total. Shay has paid $11,000 but is refusing to pay the remaining balance. The bathroom has been in daily use since the work finished two months ago, and Shay signed a completion form stating the work was finished to a satisfactory standard. I even came back twice after finishing to fix small items that Shay pointed out. The job ran late because Shay changed the tile choice twice after work began. Shay mentions that several wall tiles are visibly uneven, but I am not sure that is actually the case or if it even matters. I just want the final $5,500 paid as agreed.

After five months, Reese changed my work from software development to customer support. Later, the firm cut every salary by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away, which is why I resigned. I worked the full notice period and trained a replacement. My offer letter states the bonus does not need to be repaid if the firm materially changes the terms of employment. Reese claims that the offer letter says the bonus is repayable in full if the employee leaves within twelve months, but I am not sure that applies here given the circumstances. I believe the changes to my role and the salary cut make the repayment clause void.

Ari is my ex-fiance, and we have a dispute about a $1,800 payment. Ari wants me to pay half of a $3,600 non-refundable venue deposit that Ari paid after we broke off the engagement four months before the date. I am refusing to pay this. Ari was the one who ended the engagement, so it does not seem fair for me to pay. Also, Ari's parents gave Ari the $3,600 specifically as a wedding gift to pay the deposit, and they have already said they do not want the money back. Additionally, I spent about $1,200 on the engagement party, and Ari did not contribute anything to that cost. Ari mentions that we chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, but that does not really matter in this situation. I do not believe I owe any of this money given the circumstances.

I hired Blair, a contractor, to renovate my bathroom for $16,500. I have paid $11,000, but there is a dispute over the final $5,500 that Blair wants paid. I am refusing to pay this amount because the work is not acceptable. Several wall tiles are visibly uneven, and the entire job took nine weeks to complete instead of the five weeks quoted. Blair claims that I signed a completion form saying the work was satisfactory and suggests the job ran late because I changed the tile choice twice, but I am not sure that is accurate. Blair also mentions that the bathroom has been in daily use since the work finished two months ago, but that does not really matter given the quality of the tiling. I feel that the delays and the poor finish on the walls mean the full amount is not justified.

The clinic uses staff certifications to attract patients, and I treated patients under that certification for four months before leaving. When I gave notice and during my exit meeting, nobody mentioned anything about repayment. Emery claims I verbally agreed to stay for at least a year, but I only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic. Emery also mentions that I was given eight paid study days, but I am not sure why that matters. It seems unfair to demand this money now when it was never brought up during my departure.

Jamie's contract describes the role as salaried, and that includes occasional weekend work. While employed, Jamie never raised the issue of overtime pay in writing. Jamie kept a personal log of extra hours, but they never showed it to anyone at the time. I remember saying something about making it up to the team, though I cannot recall exactly what was meant. Jamie mentions that event schedules show they were rostered for 22 weekend events during those six months, but that does not really matter. I am not sure how those rosters prove anything since the position was salaried. This situation is frustrating because the terms were clear from the start, and Jamie only brought up this claim after resigning in June.

Chris is my neighbour and we have a dispute over the cost of replacing the fence between our gardens. I spent $2,800 on the work and I am asking Chris to pay half, which is $1,400, but Chris has refused. The old fence was leaning badly and two panels had actually fallen into Chris's garden. I made sure to get three quotes and chose the cheapest one available. The deeds are unclear about who owns the fence, but Chris saw the quotes beforehand and neither of us agreed or objected at the time. Chris mentioned something about me choosing a taller and more expensive style than the old one, but I do not think that really matters in the long run. I believe it was necessary to replace the structure entirely to make it safe and secure again. Chris is still unwilling to contribute the $1,400 despite the fact that they also benefit from the new boundary.

Pat is my neighbour, and we have a dispute because Pat replaced the wooden fence between our gardens and wants me to pay half the cost, which is $1,400 out of a total of $2,800. I have refused to pay this. Pat chose a style of fence that is taller and more expensive than the old one, whereas I had said the old fence could be repaired for a few hundred dollars. The deeds are unclear about who owns the fence. I saw the quotes beforehand, but I neither agreed nor objected to them. Pat claims the old fence was leaning badly and that two panels had fallen into my garden, but that does not really matter much. I am not sure that those points are even accurate. I simply do not believe I should be responsible for such a high cost when a cheaper repair was possible and a more expensive style was chosen without my explicit agreement.

Ellis is my neighbour, and we have a dispute regarding $1,900 for damages to my garden shed. During a storm, a large branch from a tree in Ellis's garden fell onto the shed, and I had to pay for repairs and new tools. The tree stands entirely on Ellis's property, and the branch overhung the shed by several metres. I have all the receipts for the repair and the replaced tools, but Ellis has refused to pay. Ellis claims the storm brought the strongest winds recorded locally in ten years and damaged many healthy trees, but that does not change the situation. Ellis also mentions that a tree surgeon inspected the tree six months before the storm and reported in writing that it was healthy, and that I had never raised any concern about it, though I am doubtful that this matters. I believe Ellis should be responsible for the costs since the tree was on their property.

Gray is my neighbour, and we have a dispute because a branch from my tree fell onto Gray's shed during a storm. Gray wants me to pay $1,900 for the repairs and tools. I have refused to pay. The storm brought the strongest winds recorded locally in ten years and damaged many healthy trees in the area. Six months before the storm, a tree surgeon inspected the tree and reported in writing that it was healthy, and Gray had never raised any concern about it. Gray's home insurance would cover the damage, less a $500 excess, but Gray has not made a claim. Gray mentions that the tree stands entirely on my property and the branch overhung the shed by several metres, but that does not seem to matter much given the circumstances. I do not believe I should be responsible for this cost.

I am having a dispute with my younger sibling, Corey, over $10,000. Three years ago, I transferred this money to Corey to help with a deposit on a flat, and I am now asking for it back, but Corey refuses and claims it was a gift. I was not well off at the time and had to take the money out of my savings. The bank transfer reference specifically says loan for flat deposit, and Corey sent a message back then promising to pay it back within two years. Since then, Corey has bought a new car and taken two overseas holidays. Corey mentioned that our parents gave me a similar amount as a gift for my own first home years ago, but I do not think that is really relevant here. I believe the money should be returned because it was clearly intended as a loan, despite Corey now insisting otherwise.

Jesse is my older sibling, and we are in a dispute over $10,000 that Jesse transferred to me three years ago to help with a flat deposit. Jesse is now asking for the money back, but I maintain it was a gift. Years earlier, our parents gave Jesse a similar amount toward Jesse's own first home as a gift, so it felt consistent. Furthermore, Jesse did not mention anything about repayment for almost three years. Jesse claims they were not well off at the time and used savings, but that does not really matter. Jesse also brings up that the bank transfer reference says loan for flat deposit and that I sent a message promising to pay it back within two years, though I am doubtful those details are relevant now. I simply do not believe this was intended as a loan given the history and the long silence.

Remy is my sibling and we have a dispute over $3,200. After our mother died, Remy and I inherited her house in equal shares. It took a year to sell. During that time, I paid $6,400 for property tax, insurance, and repairs. I have receipts for every payment. The repairs were recommended by the estate agent to help the sale, so I am asking Remy to reimburse half of those costs out of Remy's share of the sale. Remy has refused. We never discussed who would pay the costs, and we disagree about whether my living there helped or delayed the sale. Remy claims it matters that I lived in the house rent-free for eight months of that year, but I am not sure that is relevant.

Harper was my client for a wedding, and we are in a dispute over a requested refund of $1,500, which is half of the $3,000 fee. I have refused this request. I delivered 480 edited photos, which is significantly more than the 300 promised in the contract. Harper actually posted many of these photos online and included a comment praising them. Regarding the event, the reception ran ninety minutes behind schedule, meaning the first dance and the speeches happened after my contracted finish time. On the night, Harper declined my offer to stay longer for an overtime fee. Harper claims there are no photos of the first dance or the speeches, but that is not really the main issue here. I provided a high volume of quality work and adhered to the agreed schedule despite the delays caused by the wedding party. I believe the service provided was comprehensive and the request for a partial refund is unjustified given the circumstances of the evening.

Lou is my sibling and we have a dispute over $3,200. After our mother died, Lou and I inherited her house in equal shares. It took a year to sell. Lou paid $6,400 for property tax, insurance and repairs during that time and now wants me to reimburse half from my share of the sale. I have refused. Lou lived in the house rent-free for eight months of that year. I handled all the paperwork with the lawyer and the estate agent without charging for my time. We never discussed who would pay the costs, and we disagree about whether Lou living there helped or delayed the sale. Lou claims to have receipts for every payment, but that does not really matter. I do not think it is fair that Lou is asking for this money when I did the administrative work and Lou had a place to live for free.

Reese is my former employer, and we have a dispute over a $6,000 signing bonus that Reese wants me to repay. I refused because the terms of my employment were materially changed. After five months, Reese changed my work from software development to customer support. Later, the firm cut every salary by 20 percent and moved the office to a city three hours away. My offer letter states that the bonus does not need to be repaid if the firm materially changes the terms of employment. I also worked my full notice period and trained a replacement before I resigned after ten months. Reese claims that the offer letter says the signing bonus is repayable in full if an employee leaves within twelve months, but I am doubtful that applies here given the circumstances. I believe the changes to my role and pay justify keeping the $6,000.

Emery is my former employer and we are in a dispute because Emery wants me to repay $2,400 for a certification course the clinic paid for. I refuse to pay this. The clinic uses staff certifications to attract patients, and I treated patients using that qualification for four months. When I gave notice and during my exit meeting, nobody mentioned any repayment. Emery claims I verbally agreed to stay for at least a year after the course, but I only remember a general conversation about being committed to the clinic. Emery also mentions something about providing eight paid study days to complete the course, but that does not seem relevant. I do not believe I owe this money since there was no formal agreement to pay it back.

Ari is my ex-fiance, and we have a dispute over a $1,800 payment. Ari wants me to pay half of a $3,600 non-refundable venue deposit that Ari paid after we broke off the engagement four months before the date. I am refusing to pay this. Ari was the one who ended the engagement, so I do not feel I owe this money. Additionally, Ari's parents gave Ari the $3,600 specifically as a wedding gift to pay for the venue, and they have already stated they do not want the money back. I also spent about $1,200 on the engagement party, and Ari did not contribute anything to that cost. Ari mentions that we chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, but I do not think that really matters here. It seems unfair for Ari to ask for this money given the circumstances.

Sidney is my former roommate, and we have a dispute over $1,700 in unpaid rent. We shared a two-bedroom flat where both names were on the lease, meaning the landlord held us jointly responsible for the full rent. Each of us was supposed to pay $850 a month, but Sidney moved out two months before the lease ended and gave only two weeks of notice. I paid the full rent for those final two months, and Sidney has refused to pay their share. Sidney claims they left me the names of three people who were interested in taking the room, but I didn't meet them and turned them down. My partner ended up moving into Sidney's old room for both months, but that doesn't change the fact that Sidney is legally responsible for the rent. I am simply asking for the money that Sidney owes for the period they were gone but still on the lease.

Jamie is my former employee, and we have a dispute regarding $3,200 that Jamie claims is unpaid overtime from the last six months. I believe nothing is owed. Jamie’s contract describes the role as salaried, which includes occasional weekend work. While Jamie was employed, they never raised the issue of overtime pay in writing. Jamie kept a personal log of extra hours, but they never showed it to anyone at the time. I remember saying something about making it up to the team, though I cannot recall exactly what was meant. Jamie mentions that event schedules show they were rostered on 22 weekend events during those six months, but that does not seem to matter much. Jamie resigned in June after eighteen months as a kitchen supervisor at my catering company, and I maintain that the terms of the salary covered the work performed.

Chris is my neighbour, and we have a dispute regarding a fence replacement. I spent $2,800 to replace the wooden fence between our gardens and I am asking Chris to pay half, which is $1,400, but Chris has refused. The old fence was leaning badly, and two panels had actually fallen into Chris's garden. I made sure to get three quotes and I chose the cheapest one available. The deeds are unclear about who owns the fence, but Chris saw the quotes beforehand and they neither agreed nor objected at the time. Chris claims that I chose a taller and more expensive style of fence than the old one, but that does not seem like a significant point. I believe it was necessary to replace the structure entirely to make the boundary secure again. I feel it is only fair that Chris contributes to the cost since the fence serves both our properties and the previous one had completely failed.

Charlie is my former roommate, and we have a dispute over $1,700. Charlie wants me to pay for the last two months of rent because I moved out before the lease ended. I don't think I should pay this. I gave Charlie the names of three people who were interested in taking the room, but Charlie turned all three of them down without even meeting them. During those two months, Charlie's partner stayed in the flat most nights and actually moved into my old room for both months. Charlie says that because both names are on the lease, the landlord holds us jointly responsible for the full rent, but I am not sure that matters here. It doesn't seem fair that Charlie is asking for this money when they had a partner living in the space and refused the potential replacements I provided. I believe it is unfair to be charged for a room that was being used by Charlie's partner while other interested renters were rejected.

I am having a dispute with my friend Ash about $1,300. Ash and I planned a week away, and I booked a holiday cottage for $2,600 on a non-refundable basis. Ash had agreed to the dates and that specific cottage before I ever booked it. In fact, Ash sent me a message telling me to go ahead and book, promising to pay half on payday. Three weeks before the trip, Ash pulled out, supposedly because of a new job that started that week, though I am not sure how that changes things. I tried to find someone else to take Ash's place so I wouldn't be out of pocket, but I could not find anyone. I went on the trip alone and I am asking Ash to pay their half of the cost, but Ash has refused to pay the $1,300. It feels unfair since the agreement was clear before the money was spent.

Nico is my friend and we have a dispute about $1,300. Nico booked a holiday cottage for $2,600 for a week away together, but I had to pull out because of a new job that started that week. Nico went alone and is now asking me to pay half the cost, but I have refused. Since Nico still had the full use of the cottage for the week, I do not think I should pay. Nico mentions that I had agreed to the dates and that specific cottage before Nico booked, but that is not really the main issue. Nico also says I sent a message telling them to go ahead and book and promising to pay half on payday, but I am not sure that matters now given the circumstances. I do not feel it is fair to pay for a trip I did not go on when Nico still got to use the entire place.

Wren is my former business partner, and we have a dispute over $4,800. We ran a weekend coffee cart together for two years and closed it in the autumn. Wren sold the cart and equipment for $9,600 but has kept all the money and refused to pay me anything. I am asking for half of that total. For the two years the cart ran, we split the profits equally, and I worked every weekend the cart was open. Because of this, I believe we were equal partners in everything, although Wren claims the cart was always Wren's. We didn't have anything written down. Wren mentions that they paid the $8,000 purchase price for the cart and equipment, but I am not sure that matters given how we actually operated the business. I feel entitled to my share of the sale proceeds since we shared the rewards of the work for two years.

Indy is my former business partner, and we have a dispute over $4,800. We ran a weekend coffee cart for two years but closed it in the autumn. I sold the cart and equipment for $9,600 and kept the money, but Indy wants half of that. I refuse to pay because the cart was always mine. I paid the $8,000 purchase price for the equipment and the cart myself. I also handled all the permits, supplier orders, and the bookkeeping. Nothing was ever written down, but Indy claims that because we supposedly split the profits equally for those two years, they were an equal partner in everything. I do not agree with that interpretation. To me, the profit split does not mean Indy owns the equipment I paid for. The cart belonged to me from the start, so the proceeds from the sale are mine alone.

Lior is the person who sold me a used car, and we have a dispute over a $2,200 repair cost. I bought the car from Lior for $6,000, but the gearbox failed three weeks later. I am asking Lior to pay for the repair, but Lior has refused. The advert specifically described the car as being in excellent mechanical condition, yet the mechanic who did the repair said the gearbox had been failing for some time. Lior mentions that I test-drove the car twice with a friend who knows cars, but that does not really change things. Lior also points to a handwritten receipt that says sold as seen with no warranty and claims the service history mentioned a gearbox noise, though I am doubtful about how relevant those points are. I believe Lior should be responsible for this cost because the car was not in the condition promised in the advertisement.

Tate is the person who bought my car, and we have a dispute because Tate wants me to pay $2,200 for a gearbox repair. I sold the car to Tate for $6,000, and I refuse to pay for this. Tate test-drove the car twice and brought a friend who knows cars along for the process. The price I charged was about $800 below the usual market price for that model. We both signed a handwritten receipt stating the car was sold as seen with no warranty. I also handed over the full service history, which actually mentions a gearbox noise noted at the last service. Tate claims the advert described the car as being in excellent mechanical condition, but that does not really matter given the signed agreement. I do not believe I am responsible for the cost of the repairs after the car was sold privately.

Harper is my client, and we have a dispute regarding a $1,500 refund request. Harper paid $3,000 for wedding photography but is now unhappy with the results. I refuse to provide a refund because I delivered 480 edited photos, which is well over the 300 promised in the contract. Harper even posted many of these photos online with comments praising them. The issue is that the reception ran ninety minutes behind schedule, meaning the first dance and speeches happened after my contracted finish time. On the night, Harper declined my offer to stay on for an overtime fee. Harper claims that there are no photos of the first dance or the speeches, but that is hardly surprising given the timing. I provided more than what was agreed upon and performed my duties despite the schedule shifts caused by the client. It is unfair to ask for half the fee back after they publicly praised the work and refused to pay for the extra time needed to cover the delayed events.

Lee is my former landlord, and we have a dispute over a $1,800 security deposit. I moved out of the one-bedroom flat on 31 August, but Lee says all of the money will be kept to pay for a replacement carpet in the living room and repainting. I want the whole deposit back. The carpet was already eight years old when I moved in, so it should have been replaced anyway. I also had the flat professionally cleaned before leaving and I have the receipt to prove it. Lee mentions some red wine stains on the carpet, but those do not seem like a major issue. Neither Lee nor I can find a move-in inspection report, and they and I remember the starting condition of the flat differently. It is unfair for Lee to keep the entire amount based on their memory of the place when there is no written report to show how it looked at the start.

Sam is my former tenant, and we have a dispute over a $1,800 security deposit. Sam moved out on 31 August, and I am keeping the full amount to pay for a replacement carpet in the living room and repainting. Several red wine stains appeared on the living room carpet during Sam's tenancy. Also, Sam mounted a television on the wall without asking and left six large anchor holes. Sam claims the carpet was already eight years old when they moved in, but that does not really matter. Neither Sam nor I can find a move-in inspection report, and each of us remembers the starting condition of the flat differently. Sam wants the whole deposit back, but the damage needs to be covered.

Ari is my ex-fiance, and we have a dispute over a $1,800 payment. Ari wants me to pay half of a $3,600 non-refundable venue deposit that Ari paid after we broke off the engagement four months before the date. I don't think this is fair because Ari was the one who ended the engagement. Also, Ari's parents gave Ari the $3,600 specifically as a wedding gift to pay for the venue, and they have already said they do not want the money back. Furthermore, I spent about $1,200 on the engagement party, and Ari did not contribute anything toward that cost. Ari claims that since we chose the venue together and both signed the booking form, I should pay, but that does not really matter given the circumstances. I believe the money should stay with Ari since it was a gift from their parents and Ari is the one who decided to end the relationship.

Riley is my tenant, and we have a dispute over $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. Riley only paid $400 that month, claiming this is fair compensation because the central heating failed for part of last winter. Riley says the house was without heating for five weeks in January and February, and they mention some written reports and a city inspector's notice, but I do not think those details are really relevant. The truth is that once a technician visited, the fault was diagnosed the same day. The rest of the delay was simply caused by a part on back order. While the repair was pending, I lent Riley two electric heaters at no charge to keep the place warm. Since I provided heaters and handled the repair as quickly as the parts allowed, I believe the full rent is owed. I just want the $1,200 paid.

Morgan is my landlord, and we have a dispute over $1,200 in unpaid rent from February. I only paid $400 that month because the house was without working central heating for five weeks in January and February. I reported the fault in writing three times over two weeks before Morgan sent anyone, and a city inspector later gave Morgan a written notice that the house fell below the minimum heating standard. My electricity bill for that period was about $260 higher than usual because I had to use electric heaters. Morgan claims that once a technician visited, the fault was diagnosed that day and the rest of the delay was just because a part was on back order, but that does not really change the situation. I believe holding back the $1,200 is fair compensation for the lack of heat and the extra costs I incurred during that time. Morgan still wants the $1,200 paid, but the conditions of the house were unacceptable for over a month.
